reference.source: Scriver's OMMBID / Nelson Textbook of Paediatrics
clinicalPearls: X-linked recessive disorder caused by pathogenic variants in ATP7A, encoding a copper-transporting P-type ATPase, so affected infants are almost always male
The defect impairs intestinal copper absorption and delivery of copper to cuproenzymes, producing low serum copper and low caeruloplasmin
Presents in early infancy with progressive neurodegeneration, hypotonia, seizures and failure to thrive after an initially unremarkable neonatal period
The characteristic sparse, depigmented, brittle hair shows pili torti (twisted shafts) on microscopy, giving the 'kinky hair' appearance
Connective tissue and vascular abnormalities arise from deficient lysyl oxidase activity, causing tortuous cerebral and systemic vessels, bladder diverticula and joint laxity
Parenteral copper-histidine may help if started very early, but neurological outcome remains poor once degeneration is established
Occipital horn syndrome is an allelic, milder ATP7A phenotype dominated by connective tissue features
Neonatal screening pitfalls exist because serum copper and caeruloplasmin are physiologically low in healthy newborns
reference.pathophysiology: Menkes disease results from loss of function of the copper-transporting ATPase ATP7A, which normally moves copper across the enterocyte basolateral membrane and delivers it within cells to copper-dependent enzymes. The defect traps dietary copper in intestinal and renal cells while depriving other tissues, so despite total-body copper accumulation in some sites, functional copper deficiency dominates. Reduced activity of cuproenzymes explains the phenotype: deficient lysyl oxidase impairs collagen and elastin cross-linking (vascular tortuosity, connective tissue laxity), deficient dopamine beta-hydroxylase disturbs catecholamine metabolism, and reduced cytochrome c oxidase and other enzymes contribute to the neurodegeneration and hair changes.
additionalDifferentials: Child abuse or non-accidental injury (because of fractures and subdural collections)
Ehlers-Danlos syndrome and other connective tissue disorders
additionalInvestigations: Serum copper and caeruloplasmin (characteristically low, interpreted cautiously in neonates)
Plasma and cerebrospinal fluid catecholamine ratios reflecting dopamine beta-hydroxylase deficiency
Light microscopy of hair demonstrating pili torti
Molecular genetic testing of ATP7A to confirm the diagnosis and enable carrier testing
Neuroimaging showing atrophy, subdural collections and tortuous intracranial vessels
Skeletal survey for metaphyseal changes and wormian bones
redFlags: Progressive seizures and developmental regression in a young male infant
Unexplained fractures or subdural haemorrhage that may mimic non-accidental injury
Vascular tortuosity with risk of aneurysm or haemorrhage
Rapid neurological deterioration signalling advanced disease
reference.prognosis: The classic form is progressive and usually fatal in early childhood, with severe neurodevelopmental impairment. Very early parenteral copper replacement, particularly with certain ATP7A variants retaining residual function, may improve survival and neurological outcome, but many children remain profoundly affected.
pitfalls: Interpreting low neonatal serum copper and caeruloplasmin as normal and delaying diagnosis
Attributing fractures and subdural collections solely to non-accidental injury
Starting copper replacement too late, after irreversible neurodegeneration
Overlooking the diagnosis because early neonatal development can appear normal
references: Scriver's Online Metabolic and Molecular Bases of Inherited Disease
management: Early parenteral copper-histidine replacement, most beneficial when started neonatally and in ATP7A variants retaining residual transporter function
Anticonvulsant therapy for seizures and management of hypotonia
Nutritional support for failure to thrive and feeding difficulty
Surveillance and management of connective-tissue and vascular complications, including bladder diverticula with attention to urinary tract infection
Neuroimaging follow-up for subdural collections alongside supportive neurodevelopmental therapies
Genetic counselling with maternal carrier testing and prenatal or pre-symptomatic diagnosis given X-linked inheritance
Coordinated metabolic medicine and clinical genetics multidisciplinary care with palliative input in advanced disease
